power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: Parental and adolescent emotion regulation are associated, yet the role of parental reflective functioning (PRF) as a relational pathway linking them remains largely unexamined, particularly among parents of youth with serious mental health challenges.

Methods: Parents (N = 372) of adolescents (ages 9-19) with serious mental health challenges reported on their own emotion regulation within the parentadolescent relationship, PRF, and their adolescent's emotion regulation.

Structural equation modelling with bootstrapped indirect effects examined direct and indirect associations between parental emotion regulation (dysregulation, suppression), PRF facets (prementalizing, certainty about mental states, and interest and curiosity in mental states), and adolescent emotion regulation (dysregulation, suppression).
Results: Parental dysregulation was positively associated with adolescent dysregulation and suppression, whereas parental suppression showed no direct associations with adolescent outcomes.

All three PRF facets were associated with adolescent emotion regulation: greater prementalizing with greater youth dysregulation; greater certainty with lower youth dysregulation and suppression; and greater interest and curiosity unexpectedly with greater youth dysregulation and suppression.

Three indirect associations emerged: parental dysregulation was associated with adolescent dysregulation through higher prementalizing and, separately, through lower certainty about mental states, and parental suppression was associated with lower adolescent suppression through lower interest and curiosity.
Conclusions: Parental dysregulation was associated with adolescent emotion regulation in this clinical sample, relating to adolescent dysregulation through both prementalizing and certainty.

Less consistent with prior research, interest and curiosity was associated with poorer adolescent emotion regulation, raising the possibility that this facet relates differently in clinical, adolescent populations than in the community samples of younger children where it has typically been studied.
These findings suggest PRF facets may represent differentiated intervention targets, and highlight the need for longitudinal, multi-informant research to establish temporal ordering.

text.text: These findings suggest parental dysregulation and suppression may be linked to youth mental health, in part, through relational pathways.
However, less is known about which parent-level relational processes may help explain associations between parental and adolescent emotion regulation.

One parental cognitive-affective capacity that may help explain these links is parental reflective functioning (PRF), defined as the parent's ability to hold in mind both their own and their child's mental states within the caregiving relationship (Luyten, Nijssens, et al., 2017).

text.text: PRF reflects an affectively attuned, relational process through which parents recognize their child as a psychological agent with an internal experience that is distinct from, yet meaningfully connected to, their own (Fonagy et al., 2016).

text.text: Prementalizing indexes a breakdown of mentalizing, such that elevations indicate mentalizing impairment.
Certainty reflects the parent's stance toward the inherent opacity of mental states.

Insufficient certainty may indicate disengagement from the child's mental states, whereas excessive certainty may indicate intrusive overattributing that denies the child's psychological separateness (Luyten, Mayes, et al., 2017; Luyten et al., 2020).

text.text: PRF may also be especially relevant to parental emotion regulation because reflective functioning is supported by parents' capacity to remain engaged and regulated during emotionally charged caregiving interactions.

According to the biobehavioural switch model, heightened emotional arousal shifts parents from controlled, reflective mentalizing toward automatic, non-mentalizing modes of responding (Fonagy & Luyten, 2009; Luyten & Fonagy, 2015).

Whether this facet-specific patterning holds, however, has not been examined in adolescents or in clinical samples, where these processes may operate differently than in community samples of younger children.

Building on this framework, the present study examined whether PRF operates as a relational link in the association between parental and adolescent emotion regulation in a sample of adolescents with serious mental health challenges.

Parental Reflective Functioning.

PRF was assessed using the Parental Reflective Functioning Questionnaire -Adolescent Version (PRFQ-A; adapted from Luyten, Mayes, et al., 2017), a self-report measure of parents' capacity to recognize and interpret their adolescent's mental states.
text.formatted: PRF was assessed using the Parental Reflective Functioning Questionnaire -Adolescent Version (PRFQ-A; adapted from <ref type="bibr">Luyten, Mayes, et al., 2017)</ref>, a self-report measure of parents' capacity to recognize and interpret their adolescent's mental states.

text.text: Items are rated on a 7-point Likert scale and load onto three subscales: prementalizing, certainty about mental states, and interest and curiosity in mental states.

Prementalizing reflects a nonmentalizing stance characterized by rigid or distorted attributions about the adolescent's mental states, with higher scores indicating greater impairment (e.g., "My child sometimes gets ill to keep me from doing what I want to do").
Certainty reflects the degree of confidence with which parents perceive themselves to understand the adolescent's mental states (e.g., "I always know why my child acts the way he or she does").

Interest and curiosity captures the extent to which parents are motivated to explore and reflect on the adolescent's thoughts and feelings (e.g., "I wonder a lot about what my child is thinking and feeling").

text.text: This study examined direct and indirect associations among parental emotion regulation, PRF, and adolescent emotion regulation among parents of adolescents with serious mental health challenges.

Parental dysregulation was indirectly associated with adolescent dysregulation through both higher prementalizing and lower certainty about the adolescent's mental states, whereas parental suppression was indirectly associated with lower adolescent suppression through lower interest and curiosity.
Contrary to hypotheses, interest and curiosity was associated with greater, rather than lower, adolescent dysregulation and suppression.
Together, these findings suggest that distinct forms of parental regulatory difficulty may relate to adolescent emotion regulation through different facets of parental mentalizing.

Extending prior work conducted largely with younger children in community samples, this pattern underscores the importance of conceptualizing both emotion regulation and mentalizing as multidimensional processes within the parent-adolescent relationship (Paley & Hajal, 2022; Vernon & Moretti, 2024).

text.text: A related possibility concerns what the subscale captures.

Items index how much parents report wondering about their adolescent's thoughts and feelings (e.g., "I wonder a lot about what my child is thinking and feeling"), which reflects motivation to think about the adolescent's mind rather than the attunement of that thinking.
Among parents of adolescents with serious mental health challenges, frequent wondering may reflect worry or preoccupation rather than open, non-presumptive curiosity.
Because adolescents' mental states become increasingly private (Herd et al., 2020; Morris et al., 2017), sustained parental attention to them may also be experienced as intrusive.

text.text: Alternatively, parents may become more curious as their adolescent's mental states become harder to read during periods of dysregulation or withdrawal, consistent with evidence that parental mentalizing shifts in response to child difficulties (Malcorps et al., 2024).

text.text: Under this account, curiosity may be a response to adolescent difficulty rather than a contributor to it.
The findings for certainty and curiosity also ran opposite to the possibility raised in the introduction that certainty might be less adaptive and curiosity more adaptive in adolescence.

Here, greater certainty, which was low on average, was associated with better regulation, and greater curiosity, which was high on average, was associated with poorer regulation.I Parental dysregulation was also directly associated with both greater prementalizing and lower certainty about the adolescent's mental states, and each of these facets, in turn, carried a significant indirect association with adolescent dysregulation.

This pattern is consistent with the biobehavioural switch model, in which heightened affective arousal shifts parents from controlled, reflective mentalizing toward more automatic, non-mentalizing modes of processing (Fonagy & Luyten, 2009; Luyten & Fonagy, 2015), and with evidence that parental regulatory difficulties are associated with greater prementalizing and reduced confidence in understanding children's mental states (Schultheis et al., 2019).

These findings extend prior work in which prementalizing mediated associations between parental emotional difficulties and child outcomes (Keleynikov et al., 2024; Wang, 2022).

text.text: Although parental suppression was most strongly associated with prementalizing among the PRF facets, prementalizing was unrelated to adolescent suppression, and the corresponding indirect association was not significant.
The only significant indirect association with adolescent suppression instead involved interest and curiosity.

Parental suppression was associated with lower interest and curiosity, consistent with conceptualizing suppression as an effortful, response-focused strategy that directs attentional resources inward toward monitoring and inhibiting one's own emotional expression (Gross & Cassidy, 2019; Karnilowicz et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Parental suppression was associated with lower interest and curiosity, consistent with conceptualizing suppression as an effortful, response-focused strategy that directs attentional resources inward toward monitoring and inhibiting one's own emotional expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gross & Cassidy, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Karnilowicz et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, greater interest and curiosity was also associated with greater adolescent suppression, yielding a negative indirect association whereby higher parental suppression was associated with lower adolescent suppression through lower interest and curiosity.
This pattern runs counter to, and therefore does not explain, the positive bivariate association between parent and adolescent suppression.

Instead, if elevated interest and curiosity reflected intrusive over-attention, reduced curiosity among more suppressive parents may have corresponded to less intrusive parenting, which could plausibly relate to lower adolescent suppression.
Alternatively, adolescents who suppress less may elicit less parental curiosity, or both processes may reflect broader strain within the parent-adolescent relationship.

As parental intrusiveness and adolescents' perceptions of parental attention were not assessed, these interpretations remain speculative and future research should continue to explore these associations.
This study is not without limitations.

The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and does not establish temporal ordering; associations may equally reflect adolescent regulatory difficulties shaping parental regulation and reflective functioning, and longitudinal designs are needed to clarify their direction.

All variables were assessed via parent report, raising the possibility that shared method variance inflated associations and limiting the extent to which findings reflect relational processes versus parent perception biases.

This concern is particularly relevant for parent-reported adolescent emotion regulation, as parents higher in prementalizing may also perceive and report their adolescents' regulation less accurately.
Multi-informant approaches, including adolescent selfreport and observational measures, would strengthen confidence in these findings.
Further, whether PRFQ facets, particularly interest and curiosity, function equivalently for parents of adolescents and parents of young children requires further psychometric investigation.

Finally, this sample limits generalizability, as it represents a population in which these processes are likely to be most pronounced; it remains unclear whether similar patterns would emerge in community samples or at different developmental stages.

This study's central finding is that parental dysregulation was associated with adolescent dysregulation through both prementalizing and certainty, consistent with a shift toward more automatic, less reflective processing under high arousal.

A second, unanticipated finding was that interest and curiosity was associated with greater adolescent dysregulation and suppression, and that a significant indirect path linked parental suppression to lower adolescent suppression through reduced curiosity.
These associations raise questions about whether interest and curiosity carries the same adaptive meaning in clinical, adolescent populations as it does in community samples of younger children.

If replicated longitudinally, these findings may carry clinical implications: parents presenting with high-arousal dysregulation may benefit most from support in sustaining reflective attributions under stress, and interventions that cultivate parental curiosity may need to attend to whether that curiosity is attuned to the adolescent's experience rather than intrusive.

More broadly, this research may help refine which mentalizing processes are targeted in interventions for families navigating relational strain (Georg et al., 2023; Gervinskaitė-Paulaitienė et al., 2024; Moretti et al., 2015; Zayde et al., 2023).

text.text: Accordingly, understanding adolescent emotion regulation requires attention not only to adolescent's regulatory capacities, but also to parents' emotion regulation within the caregiving relationship.

Literature has largely characterized parental emotion regulation as a generalized, trait-like disposition, an approach that indexes whether parents regulate emotion effectively in general but not how they regulate within specific caregiving relationships.

While this work has been instrumental in establishing robust associations between caregiver emotion regulation and youth socialemotional adjustment across development, this measurement approach may limit insight into the specificity and complexity of the relational process (Fombouchet et al., 2023; Goagoses et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024).

text.text: Parental emotion regulation is also not a unitary construct.

Facets such as dysregulation, affective arousal or expression that disrupts goal-directed tasks, and suppression, inhibition or concealment of emotional expression once emotion has been activated, represent distinct forms of regulatory difficulty (Blader et al., 2025; Gross & Cassidy, 2024; Thompson, 2019).

text.text: Because dysregulation is more outwardly expressed and suppression is, by definition, less visible, these facets may relate to youth outcomes through different pathways.

Dysregulation may be more directly observable within parent-adolescent interactions, whereas suppression may operate less directly, through reduced parental engagement, emotional openness, or availability.

Consistent with this distinction, among a sample of youth with serious mental health challenges, parental dysregulation measured within the parent-child relationship was associated with greater youth internalizing and externalizing problems both directly and indirectly through youth attachment.
